title: Claude Is Now Leaving Invisible Fingerprints In Its Text (title from repo catalog .prism/shared/pot/catalog_local.json; no description file present)
core_takeaway: Anthropic is rolling out statistical text watermarking on Claude output: at each generation step the sampler secretly partitions candidate tokens into 'green' (preferred) and 'red' sets and nudges green tokens upward, so a detector holding the key can count green-token density and compute how implausibly high it is for human text. The mark is invisible to readers, survives copy-paste and light editing, and only 'eligible organizations' can run the detector. It does not identify the author, only that the text was machine-generated or heavily machine-edited, and the presenter's stated remedy is to run open-weights models you control.
key_points: The scheme is token-level, not hidden characters: candidate next-tokens are secretly colored green/red and green ones get a small probability nudge during sampling.

Detection is a statistical count, not a lookup: enough green tokens in a passage makes the human-authored hypothesis vanishingly unlikely (the presenter's example: 21 greens in a paragraph is less likely than a lottery win).
Green words can be any ordinary word and the green/red assignment can rotate over time, so a reader cannot spot or blacklist them.
The presenter states Anthropic is likely using a SynthID-style variant with context-dependent probabilities and a tournament sampling step, though the core mechanism matches the published research.
The mark survives copy-paste and light editing; swapping a few words does not clear it.
Rewriting the whole text word-by-word does remove it, and an open-weights LLM running locally can be used to do that rewrite.
The watermark does not trace text to an individual — it only shows the text was Claude-written or heavily Claude-edited.
Detection is not open to the public: only certain eligible organizations can check, which is the asymmetry the presenter objects to.
The presenter's stated conclusion is to use free, open-weights systems you run yourself because they 'work for you, not against you'.
why_it_matters: If provider-side watermarking becomes standard, any pipeline that emits model text into a product carries a machine-readable provenance signal that neither the builder nor the end user can inspect or remove, and detection sits with parties you are not one of. For a suite built on agent-generated artifacts — docs, code comments, marketing copy, digests — that is a supply-chain property worth tracking per model, and it strengthens the case for keeping an open-weights path in the stack for anything that must be provenance-neutral.
